cards.explanation: The answer is that the hand of the LORD was upon him. That's the reason the text gives for Ezra, the scribe from Babylon. "The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him." (Ezra 7:6) I've asked for plenty in my day. A bigger oven, a quiet afternoon, one more shelf. Nobody ever said yes to ALL of it, friends, so this is a big deal.

The answer is False. Ezra has company. "…he went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants." (Ezra 7:7) That's quite a group for one trip. Singers in the group, too, so I'm guessing it was never dull.

The answer is four. Ezra starts out on the first day of the first month and arrives on the first day of the fifth month. (Ezra 7:9) Count it out on your fingers, friends, and you land on four months. Four months is a long stretch, and I get tired just carrying a tray of cookies across the kitchen.

The answer is True. Ezra wants to practice it, not only study it. "…Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) Studying a recipe is great. But the real work starts when the oven gets turned on.

The answer is to teach it in Israel. That's the third one. "…to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel." (Ezra 7:10) Study, practice, teach. I like that order, friends. You can't hand out what you haven't baked yourself.

The answer is False. King Artaxerxes of Persia says, "I hereby decree that any volunteers among the Israelites in my kingdom, including the priests and Levites, may go up with you to Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:13) Notice the word "including," friends. The priests and Levites are in the group, but so is any Israelite who volunteers.

The answer is law. Ezra is sent "…to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand." (Ezra 7:14) The Law is the measuring stick here. The letter even says it's in his hand, so he's got the right tool for the job.

The answer is animals to offer on the altar. Ezra is to "…buy as many bulls, rams, and lambs as needed, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar at the house of your God in Jerusalem." (Ezra 7:17) The king puts the silver and gold toward worship at God's house. That's a lot of shopping, friends, and I hope somebody made a list.

The answer is False. There's no sending it back. "You and your brothers may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God." (Ezra 7:18) The king leaves it to Ezra and his brothers to decide what seems best. I've never been handed leftovers with that much freedom.

The answer is without any delay. The word in the letter is "promptly." The king says whatever Ezra requires "…must be provided promptly…" (Ezra 7:21) No waiting around, no letting it sit. Those treasurers got an order from the top.

The answer is so wrath won't fall on his realm and sons. That's the reason the king gives. "Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven must be done diligently for His house. For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?" (Ezra 7:23) He writes it plainly in his own letter, friends. I'd say that's a king taking the God of heaven seriously.

The answer is True. The letter spells it out. "…you have no authority to impose tribute, duty, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants, or other servants of this house of God." (Ezra 7:24) That's a long list of people Ezra has no authority to charge. Not one name on it can be hit with a toll by him.

The answer is judge. The king tells Ezra, "…according to the wisdom of your God, which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates—all who know the laws of your God." (Ezra 7:25) So Ezra picks the people who will do the judging. I'd never trust myself to pick judges, friends. I can barely pick a cookie shape.

The answer is the LORD, the God of his fathers. That's where Ezra sends his thanks. "Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…" (Ezra 7:27) The king wrote the letter, but Ezra gives the praise to the LORD. When something good lands on my counter, I hope I say thank you to the right One too.
